title: Rings and Fields

:::lede
This chapter marks our transition from groups to linear algebra. Vector spaces are among the most tractable algebraic structures: finite-dimensional vector spaces over a fixed field are classified up to isomorphism by a single integer, their dimension, whereas nothing so simple is available for groups. Before we can speak of vector spaces we need their scalars, so we begin with rings and fields, their homomorphisms, polynomial rings and the characteristic of a field. We then develop vector spaces, linear independence, bases and dimension.
:::

A group has one operation. The familiar number systems $\ZZ$, $\QQ$, $\RR$ and $\CC$ have two, addition and multiplication, linked by the distributive law. Rings and fields axiomatize this situation.

:::definition{4.1.1} Ring
A ***ring*** is a set $R$ with two binary operations, addition $(a, b) \mapsto a + b$ and multiplication $(a, b) \mapsto ab$, such that:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $(R, +)$ is an abelian group, whose identity element we write $0$;
2. multiplication is associative, $a(bc) = (ab)c$, and has an identity element $1 \in R$: $1a = a1 = a$ for all $a \in R$;
3. multiplication distributes over addition: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ and $(a + b)c = ac + bc$ for all $a, b, c \in R$.

The ring is ***commutative*** if $ab = ba$ for all $a, b \in R$.
:::

:::example{4.1.2}
The integers $\ZZ$, the rationals $\QQ$, the reals $\RR$ and the complex numbers $\CC$ are commutative rings under the usual operations. Most rings in this book are commutative. The main exceptions are the rings of $n \times n$ matrices and of linear operators on a vector space, which we meet in Chapter 5.
:::

:::proposition{4.1.3} First consequences of the axioms
Let $R$ be a ring and $a, b \in R$. Then:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $0a = a0 = 0$;
2. $(-a)b = a(-b) = -(ab)$; in particular $(-1)a = -a$;
3. $(-a)(-b) = ab$.
:::

:::proof
(a) By distributivity, $a0 = a(0 + 0) = a0 + a0$. Adding $-(a0)$ to both sides gives $0 = a0$. The same argument gives $0a = 0$.

(b) We have $ab + (-a)b = (a + (-a))b = 0b = 0$, so $(-a)b$ is the additive inverse of $ab$. Likewise $ab + a(-b) = a(b + (-b)) = 0$. Taking $a = 1$ gives $(-1)b = -b$.

(c) By (b) twice, $(-a)(-b) = -\big(a(-b)\big) = -\big(-(ab)\big) = ab$.
:::

:::proposition{4.1.4} The zero ring
In a ring $R$ we have $1 = 0$ if and only if $R = \{0\}$.
:::

:::proof
If $1 = 0$, then every $a \in R$ satisfies $a = a1 = a0 = 0$. Conversely, if $R = \{0\}$ then $1 = 0$.
:::

The set $\{0\}$ with $0 + 0 = 0 \cdot 0 = 0$ is a ring, the ***zero ring***. By the proposition it is the only ring in which $1 = 0$.

:::definition{4.1.5} Units
An element $a$ of a ring $R$ is a ***unit*** if there is $b \in R$ with $ab = ba = 1$. Such a $b$ is unique: if $ab' = b'a = 1$ as well, then $b = b(ab') = (ba)b' = b'$. We call it the ***inverse*** of $a$ and write it $a^{-1}$. The set of units of $R$ is denoted $R^\times$.
:::

:::note
The units of $R$ form a group $R^\times$ under multiplication: $1$ is a unit, the inverse of a unit is a unit, and if $a, b$ are units then so is $ab$, with $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$. For example $\ZZ^\times = \{1, -1\}$, and for $n \geq 2$, $(\ZZ/n)^\times$ is the group of residues coprime to $n$ (Proposition [2.4.9](/notes/math-55a/2-4-subgroups#proposition-2-4-9)). In a nonzero ring, $0$ is never a unit, since $0b = 0 \neq 1$.
:::

:::definition{4.1.6} Field
A ***field*** is a commutative ring $k$ in which $1 \neq 0$ and every nonzero element is a unit. Equivalently, $k^\times = k \setminus \{0\}$, so that $(k \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an abelian group.
:::

The condition $1 \neq 0$ excludes the zero ring, which by convention is not a field. The rings $\QQ$, $\RR$ and $\CC$ are fields; $\ZZ$ is not, since $2$ has no inverse in $\ZZ$.

:::definition{4.1.7} Subrings and subfields
A ***subring*** of a ring $R$ is a subset $S \subseteq R$ that contains $0$ and $1$ and is closed under addition, negation and multiplication; it is a ring with the operations of $R$. A ***subfield*** of a field $K$ is a subring $k \subseteq K$ that is closed under taking inverses of nonzero elements; it is then a field. In this situation we call $K$ a ***field extension*** of $k$.
:::

For instance $\ZZ$ is a subring of $\QQ$, and $\QQ \subseteq \RR \subseteq \CC$ are subfields.

:::definition{4.1.8} Zero divisor
A nonzero element $a$ of a commutative ring $R$ is a ***zero divisor*** if $ab = 0$ for some nonzero $b \in R$.
:::

:::proposition{4.1.9} Fields have no zero divisors
Let $k$ be a field and $a, b \in k$. If $ab = 0$, then $a = 0$ or $b = 0$. Consequently, cancellation holds: if $a \neq 0$ and $ab = ac$, then $b = c$.
:::

:::proof
Suppose $ab = 0$ and $a \neq 0$. Then $b = 1b = (a^{-1}a)b = a^{-1}(ab) = a^{-1}0 = 0$. For cancellation, $ab = ac$ gives $a(b - c) = 0$, so $b - c = 0$.
:::

:::note
The converse fails: $\ZZ$ has no zero divisors and is not a field. A commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ and no zero divisors is called an *integral domain*; these return in Chapter 17. In a general ring, products of nonzero elements can vanish, and then cancellation fails; Example [4.1](/notes/math-55a/4-1-rings-and-fields) shows this happening in $\ZZ/6$.
:::

## <span class="num">4.1.1</span> The Rings $\ZZ/n$ and the Fields $\FF_p$

Recall from Chapter 2 that $\ZZ/n = \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$ is a group under addition mod $n$. We now also multiply mod $n$: the product of $a$ and $b$ in $\ZZ/n$ is the remainder of the integer $ab$ on division by $n$.

:::proposition{4.1.10} $\ZZ/n$ is a ring
For every $n \geq 1$, the set $\ZZ/n$ with addition and multiplication mod $n$ is a commutative ring with identity $1$. (For $n = 1$ it is the zero ring.)
:::

:::proof
Write $a \equiv a'$ if $n$ divides $a - a'$. If $a \equiv a'$ and $b \equiv b'$, then $a + b \equiv a' + b'$ and $ab \equiv a'b'$, the latter because $ab - a'b' = a(b - b') + (a - a')b'$. Hence when we evaluate an expression built from sums and products, reducing mod $n$ after every operation gives the same remainder as reducing only once at the end. For instance, for $a, b, c \in \ZZ/n$, both $(ab)c$ and $a(bc)$ computed in $\ZZ/n$ equal the remainder of the integer $abc$, so they are equal. Each of the other ring axioms is an identity that holds in $\ZZ$, and it holds in $\ZZ/n$ by the same argument.
:::

:::example{4.1.11}
In $\ZZ/6$ we have $2 \cdot 3 = 0$, so $2$ and $3$ are zero divisors and $\ZZ/6$ is not a field. Cancellation fails as well: $2 \cdot 1 = 2 \cdot 4$ in $\ZZ/6$, although $1 \neq 4$.
:::

:::proposition{4.1.12} $\ZZ/p$ is a field
Let $n \geq 2$. The ring $\ZZ/n$ is a field if and only if $n$ is prime.
:::

:::proof
If $n$ is not prime, write $n = ab$ with $1 < a, b < n$. Then $a$ and $b$ are nonzero in $\ZZ/n$ and $ab = 0$, so $\ZZ/n$ has zero divisors and is not a field.

Now let $n = p$ be prime. Since $p \geq 2$, we have $1 \neq 0$ in $\ZZ/p$. Let $a \in \ZZ/p$ be nonzero. The order of $a$ in the additive group $\ZZ/p$ divides $|\ZZ/p| = p$ by Lagrange’s theorem (Theorem [3.1.4](/notes/math-55a/3-1-cosets-and-quotient-groups#theorem-3-1-4)), and it is not $1$ because $a \neq 0$; so it equals $p$. Hence the $p$ multiples $0, a, 2a, \ldots, (p-1)a$ in the additive group are distinct, and they exhaust $\ZZ/p$. In particular $\ell a = 1$ for some $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, p-1\}$. The $\ell$-fold sum $a + \cdots + a$ equals $(1 + \cdots + 1)a$, the product of $\ell$ and $a$ in the ring $\ZZ/p$, by distributivity. So $\ell$ is a multiplicative inverse of $a$.
:::

When we regard $\ZZ/p$ as a field we write it $\FF_p$. (The proposition also follows from the description of $(\ZZ/n)^\times$ as the residues coprime to $n$ in Proposition [2.4.9](/notes/math-55a/2-4-subgroups#proposition-2-4-9): for $n = p$ these are all the nonzero residues.)
